reviewRole: Codex documentary analysis, not qualified human sporting approval

studies.population: 24 healthy recreationally active men, 24.3 ± 3.6 years; cardiac output available in 17; not an Ironman cohort
studies.work: Five 3-min work phases versus 30 short work phases of 30 s, arranged in five 6-min sections; matched work rate and time
studies.intensityDetail: Power corresponding to 80% VO2peak on a 20 W/min ramp, then reduced by 5% for delayed oxygen kinetics; not 80% FTP. Relief power corresponds to 85% GET.
studies.recovery: Long condition: each complete section has 3 min work and 3 min active recovery. Short condition starts with 30 s active recovery to align work-phase sampling. This does not settle a TFCL source's missing final rest.
studies.warmupCooldown: 3 min baseline observation and 5 min warm-up at the active-recovery intensity; no TFCL 20-min warm-up plus accelerations or 10-min cool-down established
studies.frequency: Three experimental visits within two weeks, at least 48 h apart; acute protocols, not a weekly training prescription
studies.outcomes: Higher work-phase cardiopulmonary responses and time above target for long intervals, broadly similar section-average VO2; lactate 6.2 versus 4.2 mmol/L; no chronic adaptation measured
studies.limits: Recreational males; acute mechanistic contrast; equal work rates; not an individual optimum, not FTP-based prescription
studies.reasonForTargets: Explicit cycling interval recipes in the source, including 3/3 or 4/3–4 patterns; compare the actual anchors and whole session, not the VO2 label.

studies.population: 48 aerobically well-trained healthy men randomized; 31 analyzed (10 HIIT, 12 short-rest SIT, 9 long-rest SIT); accustomed to treadmill but not specialized competitive runners
studies.work: HIIT 4×4 min compared with approximately 8×20 s exhaustive running and 10×30 s maximal running; treadmill approximately 3 degrees
studies.intensityDetail: About 95% MAS, adjusted to reach 90–95% HRmax within 3 min; MAS measured at 3 degrees. This is neither cycling FTP nor proof that any HR percentage certifies measured VO2max.
studies.recovery: Three 3-min active recoveries between the four work bouts; a separately stated final 3-min cool-down at the same 70% HRmax intensity
studies.warmupCooldown: 10-min warm-up around 70% HRmax; 3-min final cool-down; HIIT total 38 min. The study explicitly separates final cool-down from between-bout recovery.
studies.frequency: 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks; other high-intensity endurance prohibited during intervention; other usual physical activities allowed
studies.outcomes: HIIT VO2max increased more than the two SIT groups; different anaerobic and performance responses. Attrition and compliance affect interpretation; not a universal protocol ranking.
studies.limits: Male selected sample, no direct bike transfer, protocol-specific training volume, no individual TFCL dose established; some SIT intolerance reported
studies.reasonForTargets: Running 1-min VMA recipe is a different dose; bike 4-min recipes are explicit transfer counterexamples despite a superficially similar interval label.

studies.population: 22 well-trained male veteran cyclists randomized, age 47 ± 6; low-cadence group 11, reported training-diary control 10; strength outcomes only 7/9; table sample labels require caution
studies.work: 5×6 min at 40 rpm versus added freely chosen cadence moderate cycling
studies.intensityDetail: 73–82% measured HRmax, not TFCL Z3 or a fixed FTP percentage; 40 rpm differs from 50–60 rpm source recipes
studies.recovery: Methods say 3-min active rest in-between 5 efforts, but also report 30 min active rest weekly across two sessions: 24 min if strictly n−1 versus reported 30. Do not choose the missing final rest to reconcile the paper.
studies.warmupCooldown: 15-min warm-up stated. Weekly warm-up plus cool-down 50 min reported; no silently reconstructed personal cool-down duration.
studies.frequency: 2 sessions/week for 12 weeks in addition to usual training; freely chosen cadence group adds 90 min moderate cycling weekly
studies.outcomes: No significant low-cadence-group improvement in aerobic capacity, cycling performance or leg strength; freely chosen cadence group improved some measures. Not proof every low-cadence method is ineffective.
studies.limits: Veteran male sample; cadence, HR anchors and duration differ; internal recovery-volume ambiguity; prior training history incompletely known; subgroup strength tests
studies.reasonForTargets: Source cadence, work/rest and power labels are explicit. The high-cadence and climbing recipes are contrast cases, not automatically supported by freely chosen cadence results.

studies.population: 24 included studies; 501 participants in active-recovery programs and 229 in passive-recovery programs; trained/untrained, 14–48 years
studies.work: Heterogeneous interval-training programs, 3–15 weeks; no single common workout prescription
studies.intensityDetail: Different studies use different heart-rate, speed, power, all-out or resistance-exercise anchors; no new TFCL domain equivalence
studies.recovery: Active/passive during repeated efforts or sets; does not test presence of an undocumented final rest in TFCL recipes
studies.warmupCooldown: Not a common standardized intervention; individual source trials required
studies.frequency: Heterogeneous trial frequencies and durations; no universal schedule inferred
studies.outcomes: Training improvements occur under both recovery modes; not a pooled non-inferiority/equivalence proof. Inconsistent participant counts occur in some tables, so primary trials remain necessary.
studies.limits: Heterogeneous populations, interventions and outcomes; primarily separate programs rather than uniform head-to-head comparison; no final-rest rule
studies.reasonForTargets: Cross-cutting recovery context, never exact-recipe-dose evidence.

studies.population: 160 adult amateur mountain-bike cyclists, 120 men and 40 women; no randomized control group; recreational/competitive mix
studies.work: 120-s fitting observations at 100 W and 70–90 rpm, adjustments until at least 15 of 18 kinematic measurements in manufacturer reference ranges; not an aero interval workout
studies.intensityDetail: 100 W during fitting assessment, not a TFCL Z2 or individual FTP/VO2 target
studies.recovery: Subjects dismount and rest while adjustments are made; no training recovery duration or final-rest count specified
studies.warmupCooldown: No 4×15 or 6×10 aero training protocol; fitting measurements only
studies.frequency: One fitting intervention, usual mileage maintained, subjective scales repeated after 30 days
studies.outcomes: Improved self-reported discomfort/pain/fatigue after fitting; no controlled causal endurance or injury effect; some table units and mean-difference fields appear inconsistent and are not corrected by inference
studies.limits: Mountain-bike population, uncontrolled design, subjective outcomes, no long aero-position tolerance or interval dose tested
studies.reasonForTargets: Distinct open posture-context study after the relay paper was inaccessible; it must not silently replace PMID27490817 or justify an aero interval dose.

partialOrUnreviewedFullTexts.limit: Post-exercise cool-down within about 1 h; review excludes short between-bout recovery. Remaining outcomes sections not examined fully in V21C.

sectionsRead: Materials and methods including Tables 1 and 2
partialOrUnreviewedFullTexts.limit: 22 triathletes, 40 km bike then 10 km run, no aerobars, model-derived INSCYD estimates; not an Ironman duration or 4×15 aero trial. Results/discussion not fully examined here.
Full XML available, but no new complete examination of this long review claimed; V21B abstract-level limitations remain.

abstractOnlyAdditionalStudies.population: 35 recreational trained cyclists, 29 male/6 female; four groups
abstractOnlyAdditionalStudies.work: 4×4, 4×8 or 4×16 min at maximal tolerable intensity; 2 interval sessions/week for 7 weeks; low-intensity additional training
abstractOnlyAdditionalStudies.rest: Not supplied by the inspected abstract; never inferred from the TFCL source
